reference.publishing: One site publishes each term. Entries with publisher sing are rendered with DefinedTerm markup at /glossary in JasonColapietro/sing; entries with publisher guitarHub are rendered by the guitar hub with no structured data, so the two sites do not compete as the definitional source for one word.

sections.heading: Pitch and notation
sections.blurb: The units every number in the app is quoted in.

entries.definition: The letter-and-number way of naming one exact pitch, where C4 is middle C and the number ticks over at every C rather than at every A.
entries.where: Every range figure in the app is written this way: your own low and high notes, and every singer's cited span.

entries.definition: The smallest step in Western tuning: one piano key to the next, black keys included.
entries.where: Song transposition is counted in semitones, and warmup scores show the semitone where your accuracy starts to drop.

entries.definition: One hundredth of a semitone, the unit the pitch readout uses for how far off a note landed.
entries.where: The studio's gauge shows cents live: 100 cents make one semitone, so a reading of −20 means a fifth of a semitone flat.

entries.definition: In a note name, ♯ (sharp) means a semitone above the letter and ♭ (flat) a semitone below it, so F♯ and G♭ name the same black key; in tuning, sharp means a note came out above the pitch you were aiming at and flat means below.
entries.where: Every note name in the app uses the first sense, written with # and b, as in G#3 or Bb4; the studio's two pills use the second, saying which side of the target you are on while you hold a note.

entries.definition: The distance between a note and the next note with the same letter name: twelve semitones, at double the frequency.
entries.where: Your range test reports the span in octaves, and the keyboard on the result marks each one.

entries.definition: The distance between two pitches, named by counting the letter names it spans with both ends included, so C up to E is a third, C up to G a fifth and C up to the next C an octave.
entries.where: Ear training plays intervals and asks you to name or sing them back.

entries.definition: The rate at which your vocal folds repeat their cycle, which is the pitch a listener hears.
entries.where: Pitch detection estimates the fundamental from the waveform, then converts it to the nearest note plus a deviation in cents.

entries.definition: One of the whole-number multiples of the fundamental that sound above every sung note and decide its color.
entries.where: The spectrogram draws one sung note as a stack of lines: the fundamental, then its harmonics.

entries.definition: The tuning standard where the A above middle C is 440 Hz, which is what every tool here uses.
entries.where: The drone, the piano and the pitch detector are all referenced to A440, the same as the recordings you sing along to.

sections.heading: Registers and the break
sections.blurb: Different ways of setting up the vocal folds, and the seam between them.

entries.definition: A way of setting up the vocal folds (length, thickness and how firmly they close) that handles one band of pitches well and gives out above it.
entries.where: The range test's climb crosses at least one register change, and the singers chart shades the reach above a voice's cited full-voice ceiling, where falsetto, head voice or whistle take over.

entries.definition: The thicker, shorter fold setup you speak in, so called because low notes buzz sympathetically in the sternum.
entries.where: The range test asks you to stop pushing chest voice upward once the top starts feeling like a wall.

entries.definition: The lighter, stretched fold setup above the break, which still rings at volume when the folds close firmly.
entries.where: Warmup exercises that climb past your transition are asking for head voice rather than more effort.

entries.definition: A stretched fold setup with incomplete closure, which is why it sounds airy and resists being sung loudly.
entries.where: The range test counts falsetto as part of your range, and where the catalog cites a full-voice ceiling, a singer page lists it below the top note; the reach above it is falsetto, head voice or whistle.

entries.definition: The middle ground between chest and head (part fold setup, part vowel and resonance) where the transition can be crossed without a seam.
entries.where: Slide slowly through your transition in the pitch studio and the trace shows whether the pitch glides across it or jumps; the Mix, Not Shout lessons practice crossing it without shouting.

entries.definition: A setup above head voice in which only a short section of the folds vibrates, giving a thin, flute-like tone.
entries.where: On the singers' range chart, a dot at the high end of a bar marks a voice with a whistle register listed; most singers never use one, and nothing depends on it.

entries.definition: The rattling, popping sound the folds make below the bottom of a sung range, with no steady pitch to it.
entries.where: The range test asks you not to count fry as your low note: the floor is the lowest note you can hold clearly.

entries.definition: The two-to-four-note zone where the voice has to hand over from one fold setup to the next, which is where cracks and sudden thinning happen.
entries.where: Slide slowly up through the zone and the pitch trace shows what the voice does at the transition; the same dip turning up at the same semitone every session is a passaggio rather than a limit.

entries.definition: Carrying a chest-dominant sound above the point where the voice would normally lighten, brightened rather than pushed.
entries.where: Singer pages mark a belt note separately from the ceiling, because the top of a range is often not belted at all.

sections.heading: Range and voice type
sections.blurb: What a range figure does and does not claim.

entries.definition: The span between the lowest and highest notes you can sing with a clear, usable tone.
entries.where: The range test reports yours as two notes and a span, and every singer page states theirs the same way.

entries.definition: Where a voice sits comfortably for most of a song, which is a different claim from the range it can reach.
entries.where: Song fit is checked against your whole range, so a song can sit inside it and still spend every chorus in a part of the voice you would rather not live in. That is tessitura, and transposing is the fix.

entries.definition: One of the eight conventional labels, soprano through bass, for the band a voice sits in and the weight it carries.
entries.where: The range result names whichever of six types, bass to soprano, has the band that overlaps your span most closely (never bass-baritone or countertenor), as an estimate rather than a classification, and the singer library files every voice by its catalog label.

entries.definition: Moving a whole song up or down by a fixed number of semitones, which changes the key without changing the tune.
entries.where: Once you have taken the range test, song practice opens each melody fitted to your measured range, and you can shift it a semitone at a time from there; without a saved range it opens in its written key and is scored in either octave.

sections.heading: Breath, tone and measurement
sections.blurb: The words for what the tools are actually watching.

entries.definition: Keeping the air pressure under the folds steady while the lungs empty: a management job rather than a strength one.
entries.where: The sustain test scores steadiness alongside duration, because a long note that wobbles is not a supported one.

entries.definition: The small, regular pitch oscillation a relaxed sustained note settles into, usually a few times a second.
entries.where: On the spectrogram, a steady ripple in the harmonic stack is vibrato; the stack jumping instead is a register change.

entries.definition: The throat and mouth shaping the buzz from the folds into a vowel and a color, without changing the pitch.
entries.where: Hold one note and change vowel: on the spectrogram the stack of lines stays at the same heights while the brightness shifts between them.

entries.definition: A concentration of energy around 3 kHz found in many trained classical voices, and the standard explanation for carrying over an orchestra unamplified.
entries.where: The tone panel draws that band as a gold column and reports its share of the plotted energy: a number to compare against your own takes, not a target.

entries.definition: A display of every frequency present in your voice, plotted against time.
entries.where: The analyzer draws one, so a bright or dark tone becomes something you can point at instead of describe.

entries.definition: A measure of how much the folds have been used, counted in vibration cycles rather than minutes, because a minute sung high puts the folds through more cycles than a minute sung low.
entries.where: The analyzer's vocal-load panel counts cycles while that page is open and on screen: a minute voiced at A4 (440 Hz) is 26,400 cycles, four times a minute at A2 (110 Hz).

entries.definition: A continuously sustained reference pitch you sing against; when your note is slightly off, the two tones beat audibly.
entries.where: The drone in Tools lets you hear an intonation error as beating, without looking at a screen.

entries.definition: Blowing air through loosely closed lips so they flutter while you sing, which makes clear tone cheap for a cold voice.
entries.where: Several warmups run on lip trills, and they are hard to blast through, because the trill stops if you push.

entries.definition: A slow slide up and down through the voice on one vowel, without stopping at any note.
entries.where: Warmup sirens are the standard way to find a register transition and then smooth it.

entries.definition: A bright, carrying resonance made by narrowing the space just above the vocal folds, which boosts the high frequencies the ear is most sensitive to, so the voice sounds louder without more breath pressure.
entries.where: The bratty nay drills in the Pro belt-prep and mix-builder packs train twang, and on the analyzer's spectrogram it shows as energy arriving in the upper bands while the bottom line, the note itself, stays put.

entries.definition: Voicing produced with more vocal-fold compression than the note needs, heard as a tight or squeezed tone rather than a louder one.
entries.where: Lessons use the word and nothing in Suede Sing measures it: the tone panel's ring share is a self-relative resonance number rather than a strain reading, so no figure here can confirm or rule out pressing.

entries.definition: How a note starts: breath before tone, breath and tone together, or a click as the folds release.
entries.where: In the studio the pitch trace arrives a moment late on a breathy onset, hooks up into the note on a scoop, and starts on the note from the first moment on a balanced onset sung on its pitch.

entries.definition: The shape of the vocal tract that sets which frequencies a note is loudest at, coloring it without changing its pitch.
entries.where: Most warmups name the vowel or sound a pattern is sung on, because the same scale on ee and on ah asks different things of the tract.

sections.heading: Color, tuning and timing
sections.blurb: The musical words neither instrument owns, defined once for both.

entries.definition: The color of a sound (which frequencies it is loudest at), as distinct from how high it is or how loud.
entries.where: The spectrogram is a picture of tone: two takes of one note at the same pitch and the same volume draw different stacks.

entries.definition: How close a note lands to the pitch it is meant to be.
entries.where: The studio reports intonation in cents while you hold a note, and ear training scores whether you sang the interval where you heard it.

entries.definition: How loud a passage is and how its loudness moves across it.
entries.where: Swell and fade in the warmups grows one note from soft to medium and back while only its pitch is scored; the breath room's steadiness score reads loudness, so a deliberate swell and an unsteady note look alike to it.

entries.definition: Notes joined so that each one ends as the next begins, with no silence between them.
entries.where: Sirens and glides are legato by definition, and the studio draws them as one unbroken line instead of a row of steps.

entries.definition: Notes cut short, with audible silence between them.
entries.where: Staccato warmup patterns break the pitch trace into separate marks, which is the same picture a lost note makes.

entries.definition: A steady click at a chosen tempo, counted in beats per minute.
entries.where: The metronome in Tools clicks at any tempo from 30 to 240 bpm, in 2/4, 3/4, 4/4 or 6/8, free with no time limit and no mic; song practice can also play a click under the melody at the tempo you set.

entries.definition: The beats played before a take begins, so the first note arrives in time instead of being guessed at.
entries.where: Song practice counts four beats in before the first lyric, which is why a take rarely starts half a beat early.

sections.heading: Technique and practice
sections.blurb: The words the warmup packs, the programs and the book use for how singing is practiced.

entries.definition: The seven-note scale of whole and half steps, numbered 1 to 7 from its root, that most warmup patterns are written in.
entries.where: Every warmup that counts its notes, such as 1-2-3-4-5, is counting steps of this scale up from the rep's root.

entries.definition: The seven-note scale with a lowered third, sixth and seventh, which gives a pattern built on it a darker color than the major scale.
entries.where: The free Minor five-note scale uses its first five notes, and the Long phrases pack sings its whole octave slowly.

entries.definition: A five-note scale that leaves the fourth and seventh out of the major scale, so it has no half steps.
entries.where: The free Pentatonic run and most of the Riffs and runs pack are built on it.

entries.definition: The five-note scale of the root, flat third, fourth, fifth and flat seventh, the backbone of most blues, rock and R&B runs.
entries.where: The Riffs and runs pack's minor pentatonic fall comes down it from the octave.

entries.definition: The minor pentatonic scale with one passing note, the flat five, added between the fourth and the fifth.
entries.where: The Riffs and runs pack's blues cell sings five notes of it, two of them half steps apart.

entries.definition: The note a pattern is built on and counted from, called 1.
entries.where: Warmup patterns are written relative to the root, and the ladder moves the root a semitone between reps.

entries.definition: A three-note chord made of a root, the third above it and the fifth above that.
entries.where: Many warmups sing a triad one note at a time, as 1-3-5-3-1.

entries.definition: The notes of a chord sung or played one after another instead of together.
entries.where: The lip-trill arpeggio, the octave arpeggio and the Long phrases pack's arpeggio chain are all arpeggios.

entries.definition: The interval of five semitones, as from C up to F.
entries.where: Ear training plays it, and the Leaps and intervals pack opens on it.

entries.definition: The interval of seven semitones, as from C up to G.
entries.where: Ear training plays it, and many sirens and leaps in the warmups span it.

entries.definition: The interval of nine semitones for a major sixth, as from C up to A.
entries.where: The free Major sixth leaps warmup sings it up and back twice.

entries.definition: The interval of an octave plus a major third, as from C up to the E above the next C.
entries.where: The High notes routine and the Leaps and intervals pack reach it, always inside your measured range.

entries.definition: A move between two notes that are more than one scale step apart.
entries.where: The Leaps and intervals pack drills leaps from a fourth to a tenth, up and down.

entries.definition: Arriving at a note from below by sliding up into it instead of starting on its pitch.
entries.where: A warmup scores a note from the moment it starts, so the time a scoop spends sliding up counts as time off the note.

entries.definition: Several notes sung on a single syllable.
entries.where: The Riffs and runs pack drills the short melismas pop and gospel runs are made of.

entries.definition: A quick melisma that travels several notes up or down a scale.
entries.where: The free Agility run and Pentatonic run and the whole Riffs and runs pack are runs.

entries.definition: A small ornament that circles one note, touching the notes above and below it before coming back.
entries.where: The Riffs and runs pack's turn and fall circles the third before dropping to the root.

entries.definition: Three equal notes in the time normally given to two of the same kind.
entries.where: The Riffs and runs pack's triplet cells fall in three groups of three.

entries.definition: A note that connects two others by step without belonging to the chord under them.
entries.where: The flat five in the blues cell, in the Riffs and runs pack, is one.

entries.definition: A musical sentence of several notes, usually sung on one breath.
entries.where: The Long phrases pack and the Longer phrases program are built around sung phrases seven to fourteen seconds long.

entries.definition: A small comma written above the music where a singer plans to breathe.
entries.where: The Longer phrases program asks you to pencil them on a lyric sheet before you sing the line.

entries.definition: The speed of the music, counted in beats per minute.
entries.where: The warmups' Adjust control slows a pattern to 0.75× of its tempo, and every song plays at its own.

entries.definition: A short pattern repeated several times, starting a step higher or lower each time.
entries.where: The Long phrases pack's thirds in sequence climb in overlapping pairs.

entries.definition: Quick syllables sung one to a note, often many on the same pitch.
entries.where: The Words on pitch pack's patter exercises score only the pitch; the words are yours to judge.

entries.definition: The two bands of tissue in the larynx whose vibration makes the sound of the voice.
entries.where: Every pitch the app reads is the rate at which they vibrate, and the book's first chapter describes how they work.

entries.definition: The cartilage structure in the throat that holds the vocal folds and moves when you swallow.
entries.where: The book's low notes chapter warns against pressing it down to make a low note sound deeper.

entries.definition: The way a sung note ends.
entries.where: The book's longer phrases chapter asks for a release that stops the sound rather than fading it into breath.

entries.definition: One note held at a steady pitch for a stretch of time.
entries.where: The breath room's sustain test times your longest steady hold.

entries.definition: How clearly the words of a song can be understood when sung.
entries.where: The Words on pitch pack practices it on moving pitch, scoring the pitch while the words stay yours to judge.

entries.definition: A speech sound made by stopping or narrowing the air with the lips, teeth or tongue.
entries.where: The Words on pitch pack starts each note on one, such as the t in tee-tay-tah-toh-too.

entries.definition: Nudging a vowel toward a neighboring vowel as the pitch rises, so its resonance still suits the note.
entries.where: The book's head voice and passaggio chapters ask for it, and the narrow-vowel warmups such as Goo octave scale lean on it.

entries.definition: One held note that grows from soft to medium and fades back while its pitch stays still.
entries.where: The free warmup of the same name scores the pitch while the volume moves.

entries.definition: A short, bright, speech-like shout of a word on pitch, as you would call to someone across a street.
entries.where: The Belt prep pack opens with calls at speaking pitch before any held notes.

entries.definition: A short set of easy exercises that gets the voice ready before harder singing.
entries.where: The warmups room has free routines from a few minutes to a quarter of an hour.

entries.definition: A few minutes of quiet, descending exercises after singing that bring the voice back toward speaking pitch.
entries.where: Every Pro day of the skill programs ends on the free Cool-down routine.

entries.definition: A note sung with the lips closed, so the sound leaves through the nose.
entries.where: Many warmups open on hums, from the Morning reset's first hum to the cool-down's quiet descent.

entries.definition: A smooth change of pitch from one note to another that passes through every pitch between them.
entries.where: Sirens and slides in the warmups are glides, scored along the line between their two notes.

entries.definition: One time through an exercise's pattern.
entries.where: Each warmup sings a set number of reps, starting each one on a new root.

entries.definition: A planned day with no practice in a program, which gives the voice time to recover.
entries.where: Every program of two weeks or more has at least one rest day each week.

entries.definition: A program day that repeats an earlier day's range test after the same warmup, so the two readings can be compared.
entries.where: Every Pro skill program ends on one that matches its first day.

entries.definition: The lowest note you can start cleanly, hold steadily and sing a word on, usually a few semitones above the lowest note a range test reports.
entries.where: The Low notes program is built to make the notes near it easier to use.

entries.definition: A voice that sounds rough, breathy or weak, in speech or in singing.
entries.where: The Belt and Low notes programs ask you to rest when it appears and, when it lasts, to see a doctor who can examine the vocal folds, such as an ENT or laryngologist.

sections.heading: Guitar and the fretboard
sections.blurb: The guitar hub's vocabulary, vendored here so the set is whole; this page does not render it.

entries.definition: A region of the neck and of pitch (the low strings, the middle of the board, the high frets) rather than a mechanism that switches.
entries.where: Lessons name the register a phrase sits in, and the same shape moved up the neck is the same chord in a higher one.

entries.definition: How the instrument is held and balanced, so the fretting hand is free to move instead of holding the guitar up.
entries.where: The first lessons set sitting and standing position before any chord, because a guitar held on the wrong leg makes a barre chord feel impossible.

entries.definition: The sound a particular instrument, setting and touch produce, separate from which notes are played.
entries.where: The clean-tone guide works through pick attack, hand position and amp settings as the three things that move it.

entries.definition: One of the metal strips across the neck, and the space behind it where a finger stops a string.
entries.where: Every number in a tab is a fret number, so third fret on the fifth string names one note and nothing else.

entries.definition: A clamp across all six strings at one fret, which raises every open string by the same number of semitones.
entries.where: A song in a key your voice prefers can often be played with the shapes you already know and a capo moved up the neck.

entries.definition: A chord whose lowest notes are stopped by one finger laid flat across several strings at once.
entries.where: F and B minor are the first barre shapes the chord lessons ask for, and they are where hand position stops being optional.

entries.definition: A chord of a root and its fifth with no third, which leaves it neither major nor minor.
entries.where: The riff lessons are built on power chords, which is why one shape slid along the neck plays a whole song.

entries.definition: A chord played near the nut that leaves one or more strings ringing unstopped.
entries.where: The first chord set is all open chords, which is why they sound fuller than anything played further up.

entries.definition: A six-line notation where each line is a string and each number is the fret to stop it at.
entries.where: Practice material is written in tab rather than on a stave, so a shape can be read without reading pitch.

entries.definition: A single movement that sounds several strings across the neck rather than one at a time.
entries.where: Strumming patterns are written as a hand that keeps moving in time while some strokes miss the strings on purpose.

entries.definition: A stroke toward the floor and a stroke back toward the ceiling, which sound different because they reach the strings in opposite order.
entries.where: Patterns are written as a row of downs and ups, and the metronome guide counts the ups on the off-beats.

entries.definition: Resting the picking hand's palm lightly on the strings near the bridge so the notes sound short and damped.
entries.where: The riff lessons ask for a palm-muted verse and an open chorus, which is one shape played two ways.

entries.definition: Sounding a note without a new pick stroke by lifting a fretting finger off a ringing string, or, in the other direction, by tapping a finger down onto it.
entries.where: Lead lessons write pull-offs and hammer-ons between two frets, so three notes come out of one pick stroke.

entries.definition: Pushing a fretted string sideways across the neck to raise its pitch, usually by a semitone or a tone.
entries.where: A lead line bends into the note a singer would have slid up to, and the Bends That Land in Tune drill scores each bend against its fretted target.

entries.definition: A finger left on the same string and fret while the others move, so two chords share a fixed point.
entries.where: The chord-change drills name the anchor finger for each pair of shapes, so the hand pivots instead of resetting.

entries.definition: A short repeated figure that identifies a song, usually played rather than sung.
entries.where: The riff lessons build a recognizable song out of one figure repeated, which is the fastest route to playing something someone else knows.
